How far the frame moves toward the model's picture. The model's answer is not added to the frame -- it is a complete picture of its own, rescaled so its luminance sits where the original says it should. This blends between the two, so both ends are real pictures and everything between them is one too. 0 gives back exactly what the upscaler produced. 1 is the model's picture. Above 1 carries on past it in the same direction, which is not something the model asked for -- use it to see what it is doing, then come back down. This is the control to push if you want more effect: Intensity belongs to the model and it decides what to do with it.
How long to spin if FPTHybridSpin is true. Measured in timer resolution units. Not recommended to go below 2. Will result in frequent overshoots

How much of the frame each half shows. A half is half as wide as the frame and just as tall, so the frame cannot fill it and keep its shape. At 1 the whole frame is there at its right proportions, with bars above and below. At 2 the half is filled and the sides are cropped away instead. Anything between trades one for the other.

How the model's work is brought back up when it ran below the frame's size. Classic composes the model's small picture directly against the full-size frame. Those two disagree by the shrink's blur as well as by the model's edit, and the composition cannot tell them apart -- it reads the blur as brightness the frame has and the model never saw. The lower the model resolution the larger that error, and it is the colour shift that shows up at 50%. Matched residual carries up only the model's difference and lays it on the frame's own proxy, so both pictures being compared are full size and the only thing that came from the small raster is the edit itself. No effect at 100% or above: there is no residual to carry and the two are identical (supersampling brings its answer down to frame size before this). From hhkbble's multi-pass work on this fork.

The filter that averages the model's above-native answer back to display size -- this is what turns supersampling into LESS noise rather than more. Sharper filters (Lanczos3, Kaiser3) keep the most detail; softer ones (Bicubic, Catmull-Rom) are gentler on ringing. The model was trained on finished, sRGB-encoded frames. The upscaler's output is not one: it is linear and open-ended. These decide how it is mapped into something the model recognises. A frame the game reports as already tone-mapped is passed over untouched and none of this applies.

The model's own processing profiles. Default (standard): the strongest. Boosts local contrast and deepens lighting, and can oversaturate or look stylised -- most of what reads as 'the model changed my game's look' is this profile. Natural: the same detail work with a gentler hand. Keeps skin tones and tonal balance closer to what the game rendered. Cinematic: tones down the shine and over-processing for a film-like look. Read when the model is built, so a change rebuilds it after a moment. The names come from community testing; NVIDIA ships no names in the binaries.
The model's own strength control, applied inside it. Distinct from detail strength above, which scales the result afterwards.

What fraction of the frame the model works at. Cost falls with the square of this, so half resolution is roughly a quarter of the time. The frame is never reduced. Only the model's contribution is computed small and enlarged, so the picture underneath is untouched whatever this says. What it trades: the shading the model adds is broad and survives enlargement; the fine structure it synthesises does not, and softens. Worth having when the pass costs more than you want to pay for the detail it returns. The frame itself stays at full detail whatever this says -- only the model's own work is done small.

What the frame is divided by before the model sees it. There is no other white point; this is the whole of it. The model was trained on finished frames where white sits at 1. The upscaler's output is linear and open-ended, so something has to say where white is -- and where the game's DLSS buffer is linear HDR, that number is rarely anywhere near 1. Measured in Monster Hunter Wilds it takes 16 or more before the model's detail reaches the frame at all, and the value that suits a shaded camp is still too small for the same game out in daylight. Too low and almost every pixel trips the soft knee: the model is shown a flat near-white picture, its answer is scaled away, and only its hue survives -- which reads as a colour cast rather than as lost detail. Too high and it is shown an underexposed one, its answer degrades, and this same number multiplies that error on the way out. Raise it until the picture stops improving. Past that point it does not plateau, it gets worse in the other direction. This was once a multiplier on a measured white point. The measurement is gone: it read scene brightness rather than where white belongs, handed the model a picture three times too dark, and left the highlight path nothing to give back. At strength zero the frame is still bit-identical whatever this says.

What the model is shown, and how its answer comes back. Off (soft knee): the default. It rolls highlights off so hard the model cannot resolve detail in them -- fine in soft-lit scenes, weak in bright ones. Neutwo composed: an unclipped curve so the model sees highlight detail, then everything above (Detail/Colour strength, highlight guard, palette). It wins in bright scenes, but the curve compresses MIDTONES too, so in soft-lit content it can be worse than Off. It also shifts paper white -- re-check it when you switch. Hybrid composed: the best of both, and the one to use. Identity in the midtones -- as good as Off there -- and the unclipped roll only in the highlights, so it recovers the detail Off crushes without giving up the midtones Neutwo does. It barely shifts paper white. Replace: the raw model straight back through the exact inverse, none of the composition -- no guard, no palette, no strengths. Gorgeous where there are no bright lights, but they FLASH in motion. A reference, not a daily setting. Hybrid replace: the raw model like Replace, but on the hybrid curve -- the decode is identity in the midtones, so the flashing is confined to genuine bright highlights instead of everywhere. Most of Replace's detail, far more stable. If you love the Replace look but the flicker bothers you, use this. Off is byte-identical to before.

Where the number that divides the frame comes from. Paper white only -- the slider below and nothing else. Right for a game whose exposure never moves, wrong the moment it does: one constant cannot serve a cave and a field. The game's own exposure -- read from the texture the game hands the upscaler. The best source there is, because it is decided upstream and nothing this pass does can move it. Not every game supplies one. A buffer the scan found -- for games that compute an exposure and never pass it on. A GUESS: candidates are matched by shape, and in GTA V the best one tracks the real exposure but at its own scale, which the anchor's ratio cancels. Needs anchoring once, and checking afterwards.
Where the wipe cuts. Left of it is the frame as the upscaler produced it, right of it is the frame the model edited.

Whether the model's colour arrives with its light. 0 keeps the game's own hue exactly -- every pixel is the original colour with only its brightness carrying the model's verdict. Game-accurate colour, with the detail. 1 brings the model's colour as well, in its own hue, clamped into AP1 so nothing unreachable is asked for. This cannot shift hue on its own: it interpolates between two finished pictures rather than adding a colour difference to one, which is what used to let a warm subject come back green. Above 1 it OVER-SATURATES: the colour keeps its hue but grows more vivid, and rolls off at the edge of what the display can show rather than clipping into a flat blown patch. 1 is the model's own colour; push past it for punch.

Whether the model's edit is applied. Off shows the clean upscaler frame while the pass keeps running -- so with Hold frame (under Compare) you can freeze a frame and toggle this to see the same frozen frame with and without Neural Rendering. Leave it on for normal use.
